connection.roles: Normal roles: the lock is the peripheral/GATT server, the phone (or local controller) is the central/GATT client. No pairing, no bonding, no encryption — any central can connect.

cloud.failure_mode: Nothing breaks — and that failure mode has already happened in full. SafeTech Products is defunct: safetechproducts.com went parked/offline after ~Feb 2023 (last real Wayback capture 2022-11), the storefronts thequicklock.com and thegunbox.com are dead, and the app was removed from Google Play. The device never talked to any of it: the only HTTP URLs in the app are those marketing storefronts plus two dead share-link templates. No accounts, no OTA, no telemetry beyond Crashlytics. The lock works indefinitely with any GATT client; the only real loss is the official app itself.
cloud.notes: Pairing is phone<->lock only; the password is stored in the lock and in the app's local SQLite database. There is no firmware-update mechanism of any kind, so no firmware images exist to lose.
cloud.vendor_service: None — the app contains no vendor cloud API at all

manufacturer_data.description: Bluetooth SIG assignment to Safetech Products LLC. NOT confirmed on the air: the app's scanner keys on a ',' + type-digit pattern in the scan record, not on this company ID. Treat a match as a weak hint.

device.name: SafeTech Products Bluetooth Smart Padlock (Quicklock)
device.notes:
Zinc-alloy BLE padlock marketed from ~2015 as the "world's first Bluetooth + RF/NFC padlock"; Li-Po battery charged over USB. One SDK (and one companion app) covers the whole family, differentiated by an ASCII device-type digit in the BLE scan record: '1' padlock, '2' door lock, '3' deadbolt, '4'/'5' Gunbox safes.
The protocol is strikingly simple and strikingly weak: no BLE pairing/bonding, no link-layer encryption, no challenge-response. Authentication is a static 4-byte password written in cleartext to characteristic 0xFFD6; after a positive result on 0xFFD7, writing 0x01 to 0xFFD9 opens the lock. Anyone in radio range can sniff the password and replay it. This matches what Rose & Ramsey showed for this family on stage at DEF CON 24 (2016).
Leftover constants in the SDK (TI keyfob demo UUIDs, a generic 0xFF00/0xFF01/0xFF02 UART service, classic-BT SPP 0x1101 constants) point to a TI CC254x-class BLE stack on the lock. WiFi-setup and Z-Wave screens exist in the app but serve other family products; the padlock itself is BLE-only with no LAN surface of any kind.
There is NO cloud in the protocol at all: the only HTTP URLs in the app are marketing storefronts and two dead share-link templates. The vendor company is defunct (sites parked/offline since ~2023, app removed from Google Play) and nothing about the device breaks because of it — pairing is phone<->lock only and the password lives in the lock and in the app's local database. The only loss is the app itself.
Research status: GATT map, session flow and discovery filter read out of the vendor app. Password encoding (raw hex bytes vs ASCII digits), factory-default password, history-record layout and RFID frame format all need one over-the-air capture against real hardware (trivially easy — the link is unencrypted, any LE sniffer works).

security_advisory.detail: There is no BLE pairing or bonding, no link-layer encryption and no challenge-response. Authentication is a static 4-byte password written in cleartext to characteristic 0xFFD6; on a positive result at 0xFFD7, writing 0x01 to 0xFFD9 opens the lock. Because the link is unencrypted, any commodity LE sniffer captures the password on a single legitimate unlock, and replaying it is the whole attack. Rose and Ramsey demonstrated this class of weakness against Quicklock padlocks at DEF CON 24 (2016). The vendor is shut down, so no firmware fix is coming.
security_advisory.summary: The unlock secret is a static 4-byte password sent in the clear — anyone within Bluetooth range can sniff it once and replay it to open the lock.

credentials.notes: The password is user-chosen, never device-issued. It is sent CLEARTEXT over an unencrypted, unbonded BLE link on every authentication — trivially sniffable, and the DEF CON 24 survey demonstrated exactly this against this product family. Treat the password as publicly known the moment it is used in range of an attacker.
stored_on_device: RFID/NFC tag ID list (padlock's RF side)

factory_reset.effect: No factory-reset procedure was found in the app or in recovered vendor material, so it is unknown whether the lock has one. The credential-rotation path that DOES exist is the password update write (0x01 + new 4-byte password to 0xFFD6), which requires knowing the current password first. RFID tags and share codes have their own delete commands (0xFFE3, 0xFFC5 on biometric models).

ble.advertised_name: PadLock (padlock variant; family names embed the type string — see identification)
ble.pin_source: None — no BLE bonding exists. The only secret is the 4-byte lock password.

methods.description: Scan for the type byte, connect, authenticate with the 4-byte password, unlock. No credential exchange beyond the password.

steps.action: Scan BLE; identify the device by the ',' (0x2C) + ASCII type-digit pattern in the scan record ('1' = padlock).
steps.expect: Advertised name contains the family type string.

steps.action: Connect and discover services; enable notifications on 0xFFD7 (password result).
Write the password to 0xFFD6: first byte 0x00 (input/check) + 4-byte password (the app UI takes 8 hex characters; whether firmware stores raw hex bytes or ASCII digits is UNVERIFIED).
steps.expect: 0xFFD7 notifies [1] (main password OK) or [1,1] (share password OK); [0] means wrong password. Codes 2/3 exist but their meaning is unknown.

steps.action: On success: enable notifications on 0xFFDA (lock state), sync the clock (write uint32 LE seconds since 2000-01-01 local time to 0x1805/0x2A2B), read battery (0x180F/0x2A19) and firmware revision (0x180A/0x2A26).
Optionally set a new password: write 0x01 + new 4-byte password to 0xFFD6.

setup.notes: There is nothing to provision — no network, no account, no pairing. Any GATT client that knows the password can open the lock. What the vendor app calls pairing is: connect, write the password to 0xFFD6, and (first time) update it with the 0x01 sub-command. Whether a factory-fresh lock ships with a known default password (the vendor manual suggests the user sets it at first pairing; a default such as 00000000 is unverified) is open question #2 — needs hardware. Three wrong passwords trigger a lockout timer, but that timer is enforced APP-SIDE only; the lock itself appears to accept retries.

rejoin.notes: There is no network to rejoin. Any controller that knows the current password can connect and operate the lock at any time; a new phone/controller simply repeats the authenticate-and-unlock flow. Losing the only copy of the password is unrecoverable by any documented path.

testing.notes: No hardware, no over-the-air capture. All protocol facts come from static analysis of the vendor's Android app. The findings are corroborated in kind — not in detail — by the DEF CON 24 smart-lock survey (Rose/Ramsey 2016), which tested Quicklock padlocks and documented the same class of weakness (static cleartext password, no link-layer protection).

helpful_urls.description: 2016 survey of 16 BLE locks; the Quicklock padlocks (this product family) were among those tested and shown to use static, sniffable cleartext credentials — corroborates the no-crypto finding here. Slides/video via media.defcon.org.
helpful_urls.title: DEF CON 24 — Picking Bluetooth Low Energy Locks from a Quarter Mile Away (Rose & Ramsey)

password change, auto-relock time, LED time, tamper-alarm config
RFID tag management and share codes (incl. time-windowed codes)
clock sync, battery level, model/firmware/MAC via standard services
fingerprint enrolment/deletion on Gunbox biometric models

no existing Home Assistant or ESPHome integration and no public RE repos were found for this family — the HA path would be a new ESPHome bluetooth_proxy + script or a small bleak-based custom component
firmware: none obtainable (no OTA path ever existed); if needed it must be dumped from hardware (TI CC254x-class SoC)
local_access.summary: The device is local-only by design: BLE GATT, no cloud, no account, no pairing. A password write to 0xFFD6 followed by 0x01 to 0xFFD9 opens it. Trivially scriptable with any GATT client (e.g. bleak).

clock_sync.description: Set the lock clock; needed for time-windowed share codes and history timestamps
clock_sync.hex: uint32 LE seconds since 2000-01-01 local time

fingerprint_delete_all.advanced_reason: Irreversibly wipes every enrolled fingerprint from the device; on a gun safe this changes who can open it. No undo except re-enrolling each finger.
fingerprint_delete_all.description: Delete all enrolled fingerprints (Gunbox biometric models only)

fingerprint_enroll.description: Start fingerprint enrolment (Gunbox biometric models only)

history_dump.description: Start history dump; 8-byte frames on 0xFFF2, end marker 8x0xE0

password_input.description: Authenticate; verdict notified on 0xFFD7 ([0] wrong, [1] main OK, [1,1] share OK)

password_update.description: Change the lock password (requires the current one first)

rfid_dump.description: Dump enrolled RFID tags; notification frames, end marker 8x0xE0

unlock.description: Open the shackle / unlock (after successful password exchange)

crypto.implementation: None. No encryption, no challenge-response, no key exchange, no BLE pairing/bonding. The entire security model is a static 4-byte password written in cleartext to 0xFFD6. Sniffing one authentication yields permanent access until the password is changed. This is the finding Rose & Ramsey demonstrated against this product family at DEF CON 24 (2016).

framing.byte_order: little-endian (multi-byte integers, e.g. the clock-sync uint32)
framing.notes: Values are single bytes or short fixed-length arrays; there is no packet envelope, header, checksum or CRC anywhere — each characteristic IS the message. History and RFID dumps are streams of 8-byte notification frames terminated by eight 0xE0 bytes.

remaining_unknowns: Exact advertised local-name format and where the ',' + type byte sits in the scan record (app parsing is crude: first literal 0x2C byte wins)
Password encoding at firmware level (raw hex bytes vs ASCII digits) and whether a factory default password exists
History record 8-byte frame layout (type/ID/user/time per the UI format string; offsets not decoded in the app)
RFID frame format on 0xFFE1 and tag-ID length
Meaning of password-result codes 2 and 3 on 0xFFD7
Whether later hardware revisions (post-2017 '2.0' Gunbox hardware) added encryption

session_flow.description:
Normal authenticate-and-operate session (from the app's lock activity and home fragment): 1. Scan; identify the device by the 0x2C (',') + ASCII type-digit
   pattern in the scan record.
2. Connect; discover services. 3. Enable notifications on 0xFFD7; write [0x00 + 4-byte password] to
   0xFFD6.
4. On a positive verdict ([1] main / [1,1] share): enable
   notifications on 0xFFDA, read lock state, sync the clock (uint32
   LE seconds since 2000-01-01 local to 0x1805/0x2A2B), read battery
   (0x180F/0x2A19) and firmware revision (0x180A/0x2A26).
5. Unlock: write 0x01 to 0xFFD9. Lock: write 0x00. Three consecutive wrong passwords start a lockout timer that is enforced by the APP only — the lock-side behaviour is unknown.
session_flow.verification_note: Read from the vendor app; never replayed against a lock.

characteristics.description: Write [sub-command] + 4-byte password. Sub-command 0x00 = input (check/unlock attempt), 0x01 = update (set new password). The app UI has the user enter 8 hex characters; whether firmware compares raw hex bytes or ASCII-encoded digits is UNVERIFIED.
characteristics.name: Password (0xFFD6)

characteristics.description: Authentication verdict: [0] = wrong password; [1] = main password OK; [1,1] = share password OK; values 2 and 3 exist in code but their meaning is unknown (open question #5).
characteristics.name: Password result (0xFFD7)

characteristics.description: 1 byte, seconds: how long before the lock re-secures itself.
characteristics.name: Auto-open / relock time (0xFFD8)

unlock.description: Write 0x01 to open the shackle / unlock.

characteristics.description: Write 0x01 = open/unlock, 0x00 = close/lock. Only honoured after a successful password exchange.
characteristics.name: Lock control (0xFFD9)

characteristics.description: 0x01 = open. Notify-capable; the app enables notifications after authenticating.
characteristics.name: Lock state (0xFFDA)

characteristics.description: Padlock/lock LED duration (exact encoding not decoded in the app).
characteristics.name: LED time (0xFFDB)

characteristics.description: 2 bytes: {alarm on/off, minutes}.
characteristics.name: Tamper alarm config (0xFFDC)

services.description: Core lock control: password authentication, open/close, state, auto-relock timing, LED timing and tamper-alarm config.
services.name: Lock main service (16-bit 0xFFD0)

characteristics.description: Write 0x01 to start the history dump on 0xFFF2.
characteristics.name: History control (0xFFF1)

characteristics.description: 8-byte history frames; the end of the dump is marked by eight 0xE0 bytes. Per the app's UI format string a record carries type/ID/user/time, but the exact byte offsets are not decoded in the app (parsed elsewhere) — layout needs a capture (open question #3).
characteristics.name: History records (0xFFF2)

characteristics.description: Format [length][name bytes], up to 15 bytes of name.
characteristics.name: User name (0xFFF3)

services.description: Access-event history dump and the lock's stored user name.
services.name: History service (16-bit 0xFFF0)

characteristics.description: Write 0x01 to dump the enrolled RFID tag list; frames arrive as notifications with an eight-times-0xE0 end marker. Frame format and tag-ID length unknown (open question #4).
characteristics.name: RFID list dump (0xFFE1)

characteristics.description: Write <tag ID bytes> + 0xE0 terminator to delete a tag.
characteristics.name: Delete RFID (0xFFE3)

characteristics.description: Write 0x01 to enter learn mode, then present the tag. Result notification: 0 = busy, 1 = success, 0xFF = timeout.
characteristics.name: Add RFID (0xFFE4)

characteristics.description: 4-byte share code + 1-byte remaining-use count.
characteristics.name: Share code (0xFFE8)

characteristics.description: 17 bytes: code[4] + startSeconds[4] + endSeconds[4] + startMinute[2] + endMinute[2] + flag[1]. Timestamps are seconds since 2000-01-01, LOCAL time (the same epoch as clock sync).
characteristics.name: Time-windowed share code (0xFFE9)

services.description: Manages the padlock's RF/NFC tag list and share codes (single-use / counted and time-windowed guest codes).
services.name: RFID / share-code service (16-bit 0xFFE0)

characteristics.description: Fingerprint subsystem status (exact encoding not decoded in the app).
characteristics.name: Fingerprint status (0xFFC1)

characteristics.description: Write 0x01 to start fingerprint enrolment.
characteristics.name: Fingerprint enroll (0xFFC3)

characteristics.description: Write 0xFF to delete all enrolled fingerprints.
characteristics.name: Fingerprint delete-all (0xFFC5)

characteristics.description: SureSet control write (Gunbox feature; exact payloads not decoded in the app).
characteristics.name: SureSet (0xFFC2)

services.description: Present on the Gunbox biometric models only (type bytes '4'/'5'); manages fingerprint enrolment and the SureSet feature.
services.name: Fingerprint / SureSet service (16-bit 0xFFC0)

characteristics.description: Z-Wave module control write (payloads not decoded).
characteristics.name: Z-Wave control (0xFFB1)

characteristics.description: 0 = not connected, 1 = connected, 0xFF = module absent.
characteristics.name: Z-Wave status (0xFFB2)

services.description: Status of an optional Z-Wave module on family products that have one. Not present on the padlock.
services.name: Z-Wave module service (16-bit 0xFFB0)

characteristics.description: Clock sync: uint32 little-endian seconds since 2000-01-01, LOCAL time (not the standard 0x2A2B day-date-time structure — the app writes a bare 4-byte epoch). Written on every authenticated session.
characteristics.name: Current Time (0x2A2B)

services.description: Used only for clock sync after authentication.
services.name: Current Time Service (standard 0x1805)

characteristics.description: Model string.
characteristics.name: Model Number String (0x2A24)

characteristics.description: Firmware revision, 2 bytes.
characteristics.name: Firmware Revision String (0x2A26)

characteristics.description: Device MAC address.
characteristics.name: System ID / MAC (0x2A23)

characteristics.description: Battery percentage.
characteristics.name: Battery Level (0x2A19)

characteristics.description: Defined in the SDK; unused by the lock flows.
characteristics.name: UART TX (0xFF01)

characteristics.description: Defined in the SDK; unused by the lock flows.
characteristics.name: UART RX (0xFF02)

services.name: Generic UART service (16-bit 0xFF00)
services.notes: Defined in the SDK's UUID table (TX 0xFF01 / RX 0xFF02) but NOT used by any lock flow in the app — likely leftover boilerplate from the TI CC254x stack or used by other family products. Recorded so nobody chases it; the lock flow uses the 0xFFD0 family above.
